AI-assisted programming in biology

Why learn to programme when AI can write code for you?

An assistant can help you read a file, make sense of an error or get a first plot on the screen.

Say your plot shows how many animals you saw at two field sites. The count is higher at the site where you spent twice as long watching. How would you plot the data to compare the sites fairly?

Before asking for a plot, decide what a fair comparison would mean.

Think of a time you were stuck making a plot. An assistant can get the code started. Once you see the plot, ask what might account for the higher count. Could it simply be that you spent longer at that site? Listen to one or two ideas, then move from comparing sites to working out the observation time at one site.

Pollinator watches at Meadow

Watch Minutes Pollinator visits
Meadow, morning 5 0
Meadow, afternoon 10 3
Meadow, cancelled 10 planned

We want to report visits per minute. How many visits did we see in total, and how many minutes did we actually spend watching?

A watch can tell you something even when you see zero visits.

Give learners time to add the visits and minutes separately. We spent 15 minutes watching and saw three visits, so the rate is 3 divided by 15. The first watch gave us five minutes of evidence, including the observed zero. The last row records a plan. Use the extracted practice folder and the Remember exercise in the chapter. Keep coursework in a separate folder.

Remember

Recall what each value in the table represents before you give it to a program.

Ask someone to describe the zero in the morning row in their own words. Then use a small example to explain how a language model suggests code.

What does a language model generate?

A large language model (LLM) learns patterns from text, often including code. Here it takes the first line of a Python function and suggests how to finish it.

The line looks familiar. What happens if you give it an empty list?

“A large language model, or LLM, is a computer model trained on large collections of text, often including code. Give it the start of a sentence or a line of code and it predicts what might come next. It builds a reply by repeating that step.”

Read the proposed line aloud in ordinary language. It adds the numbers and divides by how many there are. Ask how many numbers are in an empty list and what happens when you divide by that number. A sensible-looking line can still need a decision about what to do in a particular case.

One token at a time

A token is a small piece of text. It might be a word, part of a word or a bracket.

Each new piece of text helps shape what the model writes next.

Say “The total was …” and ask learners for possible next words. After “zero”, the rest of the sentence might go a different way than it would after “three”. A model also uses what it has written so far to work out what could come next. Send learners to the Remember exercise to run the script. Move on to Understand at minute 10.

Understand

Work out why two assistants might give different answers to the same question.

An explanation should say which assumption led to each answer. Use the two replies in the chapter after the introduction to the tools.

How are code models trained?

Pre-training. The model learns patterns from many examples of text and code. It might learn what usually follows the first line of a Python function.

Instruction tuning. It sees examples of requests and useful replies, such as how to respond when someone asks, “What does this loop count?”

Examples can teach a model how to write and explain code. Tell it what the numbers in your own table represent.

Minute 10. Explain that instruction tuning is one kind of further training. OpenCodeInstruct is an example linked in the chapter. It contains requests, example programs and information about tests. Ask what a good Python example could teach. Then ask how the assistant would know whether the ten minutes in a cancelled row were planned or observed.

Cut-offs and context

The model learned from examples collected up to a cut-off date. The information it receives for this reply is its context. The diagram shows how other open files might be included.

A library is a collection of code you can reuse. The Python library pandas gives you functions for working with tables.

If an assistant suggests a pandas function that’s changed, where would you check what it does in the version you’re using?

The model may have learned how a function behaved in an earlier version. An assistant with a suitable tool can look up newer information and pass it to the model with the request. Point out the other tabs in the diagram. The tool and its settings determine which files may be included. Ask where to find the documentation for the version of pandas installed on their computer.

Scenario I · Chat

Type a question and decide what to try from the reply. What would you tell the assistant about the cancelled watch?

Understand → Apply. Explain why two replies disagree, then try a hint on a case you’ve worked out yourself.

Introduce the three scenarios from CodeRefinery. Here you might send a few synthetic rows and ask whether the planned minutes belong in the calculation. Use the two replies in the Understand exercise. Ask which assumption each reply makes about the minutes column and what the learner would add to the request.

Scenario II · Editor assistance

In this example, a remote service receives code context from your editor. When the suggestion appears right where you’re typing, it’s called an inline completion.

Apply → Evaluate. Read the suggested line in place. Predict what it will do, then try your check before deciding whether to keep it.

Show where a suggestion appears in the editor. The words around the cursor or other material from the project can help produce it. Use the supplied practice folder and see which files the assistant is showing as context. There are instructions for VS Code and RStudio in the appendix.

Scenario III · Agents

An agent can use tools to open files, edit code and run commands. You give it a task and decide what it may do.

Analyse → Evaluate. Read the plan, then check which files changed and what commands ran.

Use the report as the example. You could ask for advice in chat, try a line in the editor, or let an agent edit the report and run a check. All three can help with the same task. Ask what the agent would need permission to change. Move on to Apply at minute 25.

Apply

Try a suggestion on a case you can work out by hand.

Leave time for learners to write down what they expect before they try the suggestion or look at the worked answer.

Check a suggestion before you keep it

  1. You watched for five minutes and saw zero visits.
  2. You cancelled the watch before it began.

What should the program report for each case?

Write down both answers first. Then try the same two cases on the suggested code.

Apply exercise

Minute 25. Five minutes with zero visits gives a rate of zero. With no minutes of observation, there’s no rate to calculate. Keep the answers for discussion after learners have tried their checks. If Copilot is slow or unavailable, use the prepared suggestion and the same cases. A third check uses a row that the program should report as invalid. Take the break at minute 43.

Analyse

Follow the values through the code until you see where the answer changes.

Ask learners to write down a running total before discussing how to change the program.

Where did the extra minutes come from?

Keep a running total of the visits and the time spent watching. Here’s the first row worked out.

After reading this row Visits so far Minutes watched so far
Morning 0 5
Afternoon ? ?
Cancelled ? ?

If the time goes up when you read the cancelled row, look for the line that added those minutes.

Minute 53. Have learners fill the two rows before revealing the faulty candidate. The totals after the afternoon are three visits and 15 minutes. The cancelled row adds neither visits nor minutes watched. Point to the part of the program that adds minutes and ask when it runs.

Agent demonstration · one report change

The diagram shows several actions an agent might take on a larger task. For our survey, ask for one report column. A diff shows which lines changed.

Read the diff. Then check that the new column gives you the minutes you expected and that the visit rate still agrees with your hand calculation.

Open the Analyse exercise and the prepared files report_with_minutes.diff and command-output.txt. Read the plan before showing the change. It calls for an edit to the report writer. Ask what the learner would do if an agent also wanted to edit the test or install something. Show the two changed lines and run the separate check in the exercise. Ask learners to predict the minutes and rate for Meadow before showing the output. Use a clean practice folder for a rehearsed live demonstration, and review what the tool can read or run before starting. If the live attempt stalls, use the prepared files.

AI-assisted version control

-    writer.writerow(["site", "visits_per_minute"])
+    writer.writerow(["site", "observed_minutes", "visits_per_minute"])

A minus marks the old line and a plus marks its replacement. This part of the change adds a column heading.

What would you check before trusting an AI summary of this change?

Read the whole diff. Then use Git to stage the changes you want to save together.

Optional practical

Spend about 45 seconds here. This excerpt shows a heading. Ask whether it tells you how the new column was calculated or whether another part of the file changed. In the optional exercise, learners inspect both groups of changed lines and run a check involving an observed zero. Staging selects the changes to put in the next commit, which is a saved version in Git. They draft a message based on what they actually staged.

Evaluate

Decide what you’d keep and explain which check helped you decide.

A check gives you evidence to explain your decision to someone else. Ask for a concrete example from the survey.

Three questions about the same change

Does the number make sense? Check how the rate was calculated.

May I send this file? Think about who is allowed to see it.

What can the tool do? Check what it can read, change or run.

These questions can come up together. An agent might open an unpublished survey and then alter the data used to produce a result.

Minute 72. Start with the minutes in the survey. If the number is wrong, ask how that might affect a comparison between sites. Now imagine the file contains unpublished observations. Who can see the file, and what can the tool do with it? If a file tells the assistant to run a command, ask whether that action belongs in the task. Give learners time to think through one case in the Evaluate exercise.

Make a decision someone else can check

Say you expect three visits in 15 minutes. The script runs, but divides by 25 minutes after adding the cancelled watch.

What would you change? What would you tell someone who had already used that rate to compare sites?

Write down the case you checked, the result you got and what you decided to keep or change.

Evaluate exercise

The report can look tidy even if site differences reflect which watches were cancelled. Ask learners to name the check that caught the mistake and describe what another person would need to run it. Follow the relevant rules for recording assistance in coursework or research.

Create

Decide what you want to learn from the data before asking for code.

Give learners a chance to describe their intended comparison. Ask what someone reading their report should be able to tell from its numbers.

Which comparison are you trying to make?

Use all the time you watched. Add the visits at a site and divide by the total time you actually spent watching.

Give each completed watch equal weight. Work out a rate for each watch, then average those rates.

Choose a comparison you can explain. Find two watches for which these calculations would give different answers.

Minute 90. Ask learners to make a choice and write the steps in plain language. In the first method every minute gets equal weight. In the second every watch gets equal weight. What happens if one watch is much longer than the other? Let learners work out a small case before opening the worked example. Once they have a plan and a check, they can ask for an explanation, try a suggested line or give an agent a small edit to make.

Try this independently

Open the final exercise. It gives you a new set of watches and a suggested change.

  1. Work out what you expect, then write and run your own check.
  2. Decide whether to keep the change and tell us why.
  3. Say what the result tells you about the sites you watched.

Your explanation should make sense to someone who has only the data, the code and your check.

Minute 110. Leave ten minutes. Ask each learner to write a check, a decision and a sentence about the survey. They can open the worked answer after recording their own decision.
